lineage_context.teaching_goal: Teach the familiar tendril-bearing, unisexual-flowered, inferior-ovary gourd architecture, then contrast it with the radically reduced stem-parasitic Apodanthaceae.

project_scope.selection_mode: Central Texas family-first module across Cucumis, Cucurbita, Ibervillea and Melothria
project_scope.note: The project contains both native and introduced/cultivated gourds. Family recognition is independent from species native-status decisions.

family_diagnostics.where_to_look_first: At a node, look for an alternate palmately veined/lobed leaf and a coiling tendril lateral to the petiole. Then find separate male and female flowers and confirm that the female flower sits on an inferior ovary.
family_diagnostics.vegetative: Mostly climbing, scrambling or prostrate herbs with watery sap; leaves alternate, usually palmately veined and often lobed; stipules absent; tendrils commonly present at the node.
family_diagnostics.reproductive: Flowers usually unisexual on monoecious or dioecious plants, usually 5-merous and radial. Male flowers have a complex 1–5-stamen system; female flowers have an inferior usually 3-carpellate ovary with parietal/intrusive placentation and usually many ovules.
family_diagnostics.fruit: Usually a berry or pepo with a firm to hard rind, sometimes softer or dry; seeds commonly flattened and numerous.
family_diagnostics.field_tip: Alternate palmate leaf + lateral tendril + separate male/female flowers + inferior ovary is the gourd-family core.

visual_lesson.teaching_order: node/tendril → male vs female flower → inferior ovary → pepo/berry → genus doors → Apodanthaceae contrast
visual_lesson.intro: Cucurbitaceae becomes much easier when you stop identifying vines by leaves and instead read the node, flower sex and ovary position.

steps.title: 1 · Find the tendril at the node
steps.look_for: A coiling tendril positioned beside/lateral to the leaf petiole.
steps.why_it_matters: This is the fastest vegetative family clue in most local gourds.

steps.title: 2 · Separate male from female flowers
steps.look_for: Male flower lacks a swollen ovary below the corolla; female flower sits directly atop a visible inferior ovary.
steps.why_it_matters: Sex expression is central to Cucurbitaceae recognition and teaches ovary position at the same time.

steps.title: 3 · Confirm the inferior ovary
steps.look_for: The ovary lies below the calyx/corolla and commonly contains three placenta systems with many ovules.
steps.why_it_matters: This is a stronger family confirmation than fruit shape alone.

steps.title: 4 · Follow the ovary into a pepo/berry
steps.look_for: Fleshy many-seeded fruit, often with a thickened rind in Cucurbita, but potentially small and soft in Melothria.
steps.why_it_matters: Fruit diversity makes more sense once the shared inferior-ovary plan is known.

steps.title: 5 · Cucurbita door: large yellow flowers and robust fruit
steps.look_for: Large yellow gamopetalous flowers, robust tendrils, coarse foliage and usually larger firm-walled fruit.
steps.why_it_matters: This separates squash/buffalo-gourd architecture from the smaller vines.

steps.title: 6 · Ibervillea/Melothria door: small-fruited native vines
steps.photo_role: Ibervillea red fruit vs Melothria small green/black fruit
steps.look_for: Ibervillea lindheimeri has deeply lobed leaves and dark orange-red fruit; Melothria pendula is a finer scrambling vine with small cucumber-like fruit.
steps.why_it_matters: Fruit plus leaf architecture helps route native small gourds after the family call.

steps.title: 7 · Keep Cucumis melo labeled introduced
steps.look_for: Muskmelon may escape or persist, but current Kew treats it as introduced in Texas.
steps.why_it_matters: Prevents familiarity or wild occurrence from being mistaken for native status.

comparisons.title: Cucurbitaceae vs Passifloraceae
comparisons.rule: Both can be tendril-bearing vines. Cucurbitaceae usually has separate unisexual flowers and an inferior ovary; Passiflora has distinctive bisexual corona-bearing flowers and a superior ovary on an androgynophore.

comparisons.title: Cucurbitaceae vs Vitaceae
comparisons.rule: Vitis tendrils/inflorescences are commonly opposite leaves and flowers are tiny; Cucurbitaceae tendrils are lateral to the petiole and flowers are usually larger, unisexual, with female flowers on inferior ovaries.

comparisons.title: Cucurbitaceae vs Apodanthaceae
comparisons.rule: Despite sharing Cucurbitales, the contrast is extreme: Cucurbitaceae is a green tendril-bearing plant; Pilostyles is a chlorophyll-free endoparasite living inside host stem tissue and only exposing flowers/fruits.

visual_lesson.caveat: Tendrils can be reduced or absent in some Cucurbitaceae, and fruit size varies enormously. Reproductive characters are the safest confirmation.
